steps.title: The two limits of the disc equation
steps.answers: What does the disc equation predict at very low and very high prey density?
steps.opens: How do you estimate a and Th from data?
steps.statement: When prey are scarce Ha ≈ aHT (the straight start, slope a × T = 0.5); when prey are abundant Ha → T ÷ Th = 10 (the plateau).

explain.text: The denominator 1 + aHTh compares the two uses of time. If aHTh is much smaller than 1, handling is negligible and the predator eats in proportion to prey. If it is much larger than 1, handling fills the day and the prey density no longer matters. With a = 0.5 and Th = 0.1 the switch happens around aHTh = 1, at H = 20.

figure.caption: The disc equation (a = 0.5, Th = 0.1, T = 1) between its two limits.

steps.intuition: At first the fox is limited by finding rabbits, later by eating them.

right.title: Instead
right.text: Scarce prey: search limits; abundant prey: handling limits.

steps.misconception: The plateau depends on prey density.

right.title: Instead
right.text: The ceiling is T ÷ Th whatever H is.

check.q: At what H does aHTh = 1 for a = 0.5, Th = 0.1?

steps.title: Why the straight-line fit is only a start
steps.answers: How exact is the straight-line fit with real, noisy data?
steps.opens: How would you fit a Type III response, and which type fits your predator?
steps.statement: Taking 1/Ha magnifies the noise of small catches, so the line is best used for starting values; a nonlinear fit of the curve itself, nls(), is the usual final step.

explain.text: With real counts, a predator that ate 1 or 2 prey gives 1/Ha = 1 or 0.5, and a single prey more or less changes 1/Ha a lot, while large catches barely move it. Least squares on the transformed scale therefore listens most to the noisiest points. Fitting Ha = aHT/(1 + aHTh) directly by nonlinear least squares, with the line's a and Th as starting values, avoids that.

lines.code: fit2 <- nls(Ha ~ a*H*T/(1 + a*H*Th), start = list(a = 0.5, Th = 0.1))
lines.explain: fit the disc equation itself, starting from the straight-line estimates

code.interpret: With the sheet's exact values both fits agree: a = 0.5, Th = 0.1.

examples.title: Nonlinear fitting of functional responses (added)
examples.problem: Why do ecologists prefer nonlinear fits for functional responses?

solution.text: Linearisations distort the error structure; nonlinear least squares (or maximum likelihood) fit the curve on the original scale.

examples.answer: Use the line for starting values, then nls() or a likelihood fit.

source.title: Nonlinear curve fitting: predation and functional response curves
source.note: chapter in Design and Analysis of Ecological Experiments, Oxford University Press

terms.meaning: nonlinear least squares: fits a curve with parameters directly

steps.intuition: Turning numbers upside down also turns their errors upside down.

right.title: Instead
right.text: Small catches become the loudest points after 1/Ha.

steps.misconception: If the line fits, the transformation is harmless.

wrong.title: Mistaken
wrong.text: A straight line on 1/Ha is the best estimate.

right.title: Instead
right.text: Use it to start; finish with nls().

check.q: Which points dominate a least-squares fit of 1/Ha?
check.a: Those with small Ha: their 1/Ha values are large and vary most.
